review: The hymn is Ps 73:23–24 (בְּיַד־יְמִינְךָ אֶחֱזֶה / תַּנְחֵנִי) held together with Ps 139:24 and 2 Cor 12:9: 1:1 asks to be led, 1:3–4 asks only to follow, 2:1–2 rests the weak will on mercy, and 3:3–4 repeats the opening at the rapture. The refrain-like first line of stanza 1 returns as 3:3 by design.

1:4 וּבַאֲשֶׁר תּוֹלִיכֵנִי, אֲנִי עִמָּךְ — the Arabic وَحَيْثُمَا تَسِرْ بِي أَنَا مَعَك is not a promise to walk beside Him but the child's answer 'wherever You take me, I am with You'; the Hebrew keeps the order of the Arabic so the clause still answers 1:3 rather than repeating it.

2:1 בְּחָלְשִׁי — the Arabic فِي الضَّعْفِ is 2 Cor 12:9's ἀσθένεια; the Hebrew uses the noun חֻלְשָׁה elsewhere in this corpus, but here the prepositional clause needs the infinitive-with-suffix, since a bare noun would make the line a statement about weakness rather than the occasion of strength.

2:4 אָלִין בֶּטַח — the Arabic أَبِيتُ مُطْمَئِنًّا is 'I lodge secure'; לוּן is the biblical verb for spending the night (Ps 30:6, בָּעֶרֶב יָלִין בֶּכִי), so the line keeps the nightly image and does not slide into a general 'I rest'.

3:2 אַחֲרִית טוֹבָה — the Arabic حُسْنَ الْخِتَام is 'a fair ending'; אַחֲרִית is the biblical word for the last thing (Prov 14:12, וְאַחֲרִיתָהּ דַּרְכֵי־מָוֶת), and the adjective is kept because the line asks for a good end and not merely an end.
